claims.text: The initially solid Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles are equiatomic.
As-synthesized Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles possess a high density of grain boundaries and other structural defects.
Subsolidus annealing at about 500 °C reduces the nanoparticles' defect density.
The proposed annealing can reduce defect density without changing overall chemical homogeneity.
Grain boundaries and other nanoscale defects locally lower cohesive energy in these nanoparticles.
Grain or interphase boundaries can be associated with local defect populations in high-entropy-alloy materials.
Structural defects provide energetically favorable sites for the initiation of atomic mobility and premelting.
A higher defect density lowers the effective local melting temperature.
High-defect nanoparticles will begin premelting at a lower temperature than annealed, defect-reduced nanoparticles.
High-defect nanoparticles will exhibit a broader melting transition than annealed, defect-reduced nanoparticles.
Annealed nanoparticles with fewer defects will exhibit a higher and more abrupt melting transition.
Elemental segregation during elevated-temperature treatment can modify grain-boundary energetics and microstructural stability in high-entropy-alloy materials.
Compositional variability may affect local defect density in chemically complex high-entropy-alloy material.
The proposed mechanism is intended to apply from premelting onset through complete melting, provided significant compositional inhomogeneity is absent.
A lack of statistically significant differences in both melting onset and transition width between chemically homogeneous high- and low-defect particles would falsify the defect-driven hypothesis.
